newsitem.title: USA: No decision yet on Bosnia force, Perry says.
newsitem.headline: No decision yet on Bosnia force, Perry says.

text.p: U.S. Defence Secretary William Perry told hostile Republican senators on Thursday that President Bill Clinton had made no decision on whether to send U.S. peacekeeping troops to Bosnia again next year.

To scathing criticism, Perry denied that 5,000 fresh U.S. troops who will begin entering Bosnia within days to cover the removal of 15,800 American troops now there are a planned vanguard for any new international force in Bosnia next year.

But he testified to the Senate Armed Services Committee that "the international interest in Bosnia has not ended," and left wide open the possibility that U.S. troops could be part of any new multi-national peacekeeping force in 1997.

"I can assure you I have made no recommendation to the president on a follow-on force. He has made no decision on a follow-on force at this time," Perry said, adding that NATO was studying whether to sponsor a new force in Bosnia.

With Clinton facing a re-election vote against challenger Bob Dole on November 5, Republican senators slammed the plan to send in the covering force, especially after Joint Chiefs of Staff Chairman General John Shalikashvili testified that the troops would remain until mid-March.

They accused Clinton of violating a promise to remove U.S. forces from Bosnia by December 20 under the Dayton peace accord and questioned whether they represented a commitment by the United States to go back to Bosnia.
"Gentlemen, the credibility gap between you and the Congress is as wide as the Grand Canyon," said Republican Sen. John McCain of Arizona.
Republicans have demanded that Congress have a final say on whether U.S. forces are again committed to Bosnia.

The current NATO-led peace implementation force (IFOR) of 52,000 in Bosnia is scheduled to pull out of Bosnia late this year. While no formal decision has been made, many allies are calling for a new force in the troubled country next year and have said U.S. troops would be required.

That pull-out date was originally scheduled for December 20, but has slipped by weeks until early next year because an adequate force was being kept longer to help keep peace during municipal elections in November.
Democrat Clinton leads Republican challenger Dole comfortably in the polls, but surveys also show that many Americans would oppose returning Americans troops to Bosnia in any new force next year.
"The fact that we still have no exit strategy is still foreboding for the United States," Republican Senator Dirk Kempthorne of Idaho said at the hearing.

Using the long and bitter U.S. military experience in Vietnam as an example, Kempthorne and others asked why a covering force was needed to help remove an original force that would not be out until January or February.
They noted that Perry and other administration officials repeatedly assured the committee last December that a year in Bosnia would be enough for the success of IFOR.

Virginia Sen. John Warner noted that former U.S. peace negotiator to Bosnia, Richard Holbrooke, told the committee last December 7: "We think a year is sufficient. If a year does not work, two, three or five years will not do it either."
Holbrooke and retired U.S. Navy Admiral Leighton Smith, who headed IOFOR until this summer, told Congress earlier this week that peace in Bosnia would require a new peacekeeping force next year.
